[[Balkans]] | creator = | course = | type = Soup | served = Hot }} '''Goulash''' ({{langx|hu|Gulyás}}, {{IPA|hu|ˈgujaːʃlɛvɛʃ|audio=Hungarian says Gulyás leves.wav}}) is a meal made of meat and vegetables seasoned with [[paprika]]{{cite web |title=Goulash |url=https://www.bbcgoodfood.com/search/recipes?q=goulash |website=BBC Good Food |access-date=26 December 2020}} and other spices.{{cite book |first=Karoly |last=Gundel |title=Gundel's Hungarian cookbook |publisher=Corvina |location=Budapest |year=1992 |isbn=963-13-3600-X |oclc=32227400 |page=20}} Originating in [[Hungary]], goulash is a common meal predominantly eaten in [[Central Europe]] but also in other parts of Europe. It is one of the [[Cuisine of hungary|national dishes of Hungary]] and a symbol of the country.Gil Marks, [https://books.google.com/books?id=ojc4Uker_V0C&pg=PA234 Encyclopedia of Jewish Food], John Wiley & Sons, 2010, p. 234{{cite web|url=http://away.com/feature/excerpt/national-geographic/top-ten-great-national-dishes-1.html?page=1|title=Orbitz Travel: Vacations, Cheap Flights, Airline Tickets & Airfares|website=away.com|access-date=14 October 2011|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130117110045/http://away.com/feature/excerpt/national-geographic/top-ten-great-national-dishes-1.html?page=1|archive-date=17 January 2013|url-status=dead}}{{Cite web|date=2011-09-13|title=Top 10 National Dishes -- National Geographic|url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/travel/top-10/national-food-dishes/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161014060413/http://www.nationalgeographic.com/travel/top-10/national-food-dishes/|url-status=dead|archive-date=14 October 2016|access-date=2020-08-08|website=Travel|language=en}} Its origins may be traced back as far as the 10th century to stews eaten by Hungarian shepherds. At that time, the cooked and flavoured meat was sun-dried and packed into bags produced from sheep's stomachs, needing only water to make it into a meal.[https://books.google.com/books?id=Pf6cAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA356 Bulgaria, Hungary, Poland, Romania, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia], Britannica Educational Publishing, 2013, p. 94 Earlier versions of goulash did not include paprika, as it was not introduced to Europe until the 16th century.
